answer: So I’ve been doing a lot of customer interviews lately, and one thing I’ve learned is that the bigger the deal, the more important it is to understand the social contract. What do I mean? Well, in the early days, you can get away with a lot. You can be late to a meeting. You can have a broken website. You can have a few bugs. You can be a bit sloppy. But as you scale, the customer expectations go up. And the social contract is the set of expectations you have to meet. And the bigger the deal, the more expectations there are. And the more important it is to understand them. And the more important it is to be clear on who’s responsible for what. So what’s the social contract with a CIO? It’s a big deal, but it’s not necessarily a huge deal. It’s not a multi-year, multi-million dollar deal. But it’s a big deal. And the social contract is you have to be reliable, responsive, and responsible. You have to be there for them. And you have to be able to scale. And you have to be able to do it all for a long time. So what does this mean in practice? Well, here are a few things I’ve learned: First, you have to be there for them. You have to be responsive. You have to be available. answer: The agent was still running. Still processing. Still making decisions. Just not making the decisions we’d trained it on. And we had no idea. Here’s what happened: We’d trained the agent on our outbound process. It knew our ICP cold. It knew our messaging. It knew our follow-up cadences. We’d run it for months. It was working. Then we got busy. We had a product launch. We had a new VP coming in. We had a million other things. We stopped checking in. We stopped reviewing the output. We stopped asking the questions that would have caught this. And the agent just kept running. It kept sending emails. It kept booking meetings. It kept doing the work. Just not the work we’d trained it on. The problem wasn’t the agent. The problem was us. We’d trained it. We’d deployed it. And then we’d forgotten it existed.
